extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners (Office personnel) and patent practitioners (applicants' counsel)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness of claimed species or subgenera in view of prior-art genera, with special focus on chemical and biotechnological compounds. Instructs examiners how to weigh size of genus, structural similarity, properties/utilities, predictability, methods of making, and applicant rebuttal evidence when making prima facie obviousness findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the Size of the Genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the size of the prior art genus, bearing in mind that size alone cannot support an obviousness rejection; however, a genus may be so small that, when considered in light of the totality of the circumstances, it would anticipate the claimed species or subgenus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply a per se rule based solely on number of members. Examine total circumstances (e.g., limited variations in formula, few alternatives for substituents, unchanging parent nucleus). A very small, limited genus may make each member envisagable (In re Petering). Compare cases (Petering, Schaumann, Ruschig) and explain why size leads or does not lead to anticipation/obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the Express Teachings
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art reference expressly teaches a particular reason to select the claimed species or subgenus, Office personnel should point out the express disclosure and explain why it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill to select the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit statements such as recognized equivalence or co-administration examples (e.g., Merck & Co. v. Biocraft). If one reference specifically refers to another (In re Kemps), explain how the express teaching provides motivation to select the species/subgenus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the Teachings of Structural Similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any teachings of a 'typical,' 'preferred,' or 'optimum' species or subgenus within the disclosed genus: if such a species is structurally similar to the claimed species, its disclosure may provide a reason for one of ordinary skill to choose the claimed species from the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the number of variables to be selected/modified and the nature/significance of structural differences. Structural similarity often supports a reasonable expectation of shared properties (Dillon, Deuel). Conversely, a disclosed preferred species significantly different in structure may teach away. Use chemical-case concepts (homologs, isomers, bioisosteres) and cite cases reversing or affirming obviousness based on similarity (Jones, Baird, Dillon, Merck).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the Teachings of Similar Properties or Uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the properties and utilities of structurally similar prior-art species or subgenera because properties/utilities provide practical motivation to make related species; lack of known useful properties weighs against motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed invention and prior-art species share any useful property, that generally motivates selection. Prior art need not disclose a newly discovered property to support a prima facie case. Very close structural similarity may permit presuming similar properties (Dillon, Grabiak). Conversely, if prior-art compounds lack utility or have opposite utilities, this weighs against obviousness (Albrecht, Stemniski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the Predictability of the Technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the predictability of the technology: in unpredictable arts, structurally similar species are less likely to render a claimed species obvious because similar structure may not imply similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a reasonable expectation of success exists; obviousness does not require absolute predictability, only a reasonable expectation (O’Farrell). Use field-specific evidence of unpredictability (May, Schechter) to rebut presumed similarity-based obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Any Other Teaching To Support Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The listed categories (size of genus, express teachings, structural similarity, properties, predictability) are not exclusive; Office personnel should consider the totality of evidence and any other relevant teachings that could support selection of the species or subgenus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unusual cases, identify and analyze other relevant teachings in the reference(s). Do not limit analysis to enumerated categories; weigh all evidence holistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Express Fact-Findings and Determine Whether They Support a Prima Facie Case
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on the whole evidence, make express fact-findings relating to the Graham factors, focusing primarily on the prior-art teachings discussed, and specifically articulate what teachings or suggestions in the prior art would have motivated selection of the claimed species or subgenus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-findings should state which teachings/suggestions provide motivation and then determine whether, considered as a whole, they support a prima facie case of obviousness. Cite In re Bell, In re Kulling, Panduit. Explicitly tie teachings to the motivation/suggestion analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection Based on Close Structural Similarity (foundational expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be made when chemical compounds have very close structural similarities and similar utilities, based on the expectation that compounds similar in structure will have similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting obviousness from close structural similarity, explain the expectation that structural similarity implies similar function (In re Payne, Papesch, Dillon). Provide factual basis showing chemistry/structure-function relation rather than mere assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology and Isomerism Must Be Considered With All Other Relevant Facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Position isomers and homologs are generally of sufficiently close structural similarity that a presumed expectation exists they possess similar properties, but such relationships must be weighed with all other facts in determining obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate homology/isomerism automatically with prima facie obviousness; consider distance (e.g., far-removed homologs may not be expected to share properties) and other contextual facts (Langer, Mills, Wilder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of True Homologous/Isomeric Relationship Is Not Controlling
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art structures do not have to be true homologs or isomers to render structurally similar compounds prima facie obvious; non-homologous but closely similar structures with similar properties can suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate overall structural and functional closeness (Payne, Mayne, Merck, Dillon). Similarly, note cases where substitution (e.g., thioester for ester) did not render a compound obvious (Grabiak).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or Absence of Prior-Art Suggestion of Method of Making May Be Relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence—or absence—of a suitably operative, obvious process for making a composition may bear on whether that composition is obvious; absence of a known/obvious method to make a compound may overcome presumption of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making the claimed compound at the time of invention, the compound may not be in the public possession (Hoeksema, Maloney). Consider whether a disclosed method for a related compound would enable production of the claimed compound; methodology can be proper in rejecting product claims, depending on facts (Goldgaber, Payne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of Obviousness Overcome When No Reasonable Expectation of Similar Properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption of obviousness based on structurally similar references may be overcome where evidence shows there is no reasonable expectation that structurally similar compounds will have similar properties (i.e., unpredictability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may produce evidence demonstrating unpredictability in the art to rebut presumption (May, Schechter). Use experimental or literature evidence showing lack of predictability of properties to weigh against prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: If Prior-Art Compounds Have No Utility or Only as Intermediates, They May Not Render Claim Prima Facie Obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art does not teach any specific or significant utility for disclosed compounds, or discloses them only as intermediates, the prior art is unlikely to render structurally similar claims prima facie obvious absent a reason an ordinary artisan would make or investigate such compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether prior-art compounds had recognized useful properties or were merely intermediates; if intermediates, an artisan would not ordinarily stop synthesis to investigate utility (Stemniski, Albrecht, Lalu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima Facie Case Rebuttable by Evidence of Superior or Unexpected Results
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness based on structural similarity is rebuttable by proof that the claimed compounds possess unexpectedly advantageous or superior properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require objective evidence (affidavits, comparative data) showing unexpected properties (Papesch, Wiechert, Dillon). Mere recognition of a benefit by applicant is insufficient if the prior-art compound actually possessed that benefit. Unexpected results must be supported by evidence (Mayne) and may overcome a prima facie case if commensurate in scope with the claim (Chupp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Applicant’s Rebuttal Arguments and Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prima facie case is established, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut with arguments and/or evidence (specification, affidavits/declarations, counsel submissions), but arguments of counsel cannot substitute for factually supported objective evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all rebuttal evidence, including secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others), declarations from skilled artisans, evidence of copying, state of the art, level of skill, and methods of making. Require nexus between the evidence and the claimed invention for substantial weight; evidence must be commensurate in scope with the claimed invention. Examiners should weigh proffered evidence and avoid giving evidence no weight without reason (Soni, Piasecki, Beattie, GPAC, Huang, Kulling, Grasselli, Chupp, Hoeksema).
